exemplar.title: What strong work looks like
exemplar.intro: Here is how a strong planner explains a different event — a school field day — so you can see the moves, not the answers.

traits.sample: I divided 738 guests by 24 seats per table to get 30 remainder 18. Because the 18 remaining guests still need seats, I ordered 31 tables so nobody is left standing.
traits.why: Naming the quotient and explaining what the remainder means shows deep division sense and earns top marks.

traits.sample: I shifted the decimal point two places to turn $58.50 ÷ $2.25 into 5850 ÷ 225 = 26 packs. Multiplying by a power of 10 keeps the quotient equivalent.
traits.why: Showing the power-of-10 shift proves the algorithm was understood conceptually, not guessed.

traits.trait: Connects math to the real decision
traits.sample: For the banner ribbon, dividing 12 meters by 3/4 meter gave 12 × (4/3) = 16 banners. Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 produces more pieces than wholes.
traits.why: Connecting the reciprocal to piece size justifies why division creates more pieces.

traits.sample: I checked reasonableness: 738 is close to 720, and 720 ÷ 24 = 30, so 31 tables is extremely reasonable.
traits.why: Estimation checks catch computation errors and show expert number sense.

err-explain: The helper multiplied by 3/4 instead of dividing, but dividing asks how many 3/4-meter pieces fit, so ___.
